sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source straddles the south-western shoulder of southern Calabria, near the termination of the Italian peninsula, toward the Gioia Tauro plain. This source is a low-angle, NW-dipping, fault almost at the southwestern end of the extensional axis that runs along the southern Apennines.
Historical catalogues (Boschi et al., 2000; Gruppo di Lavoro CPTI, 2004; Guidoboni et al., 2007) show a remarkable concentration of damaging earthquakes in the area. In particular, this region has been struck, from north to south, by the: 8 September 1905 (Mw 7.1, Calabria), 13 October 1791 (Mw 5.9, Calabria Centrale), 7 December 1743 (Mw 5.8, Calabria Meridionale), 7 March 1928 (Mw 5.9, Capo Vaticano), 5 February 1783 (Mw 6.9, Calabria), and 16 November 1894 (Mw 6.0, Calabria Meridionale).
The catastrophic multiple earthquake of 1783 has posed several issues concerning the causative structure(s) of such a remarkable sequence. In fact, the 1783 seismic crisis is only one of the so many other damaging earthquakes that have occurred throughout the region, thus making earthquake geology a particularly arduous task, all the more complicated by the elusive geology of southern Calabria. One could say that "too many" earthquakes have occurred in "too little space", considering the size of earthquake faulting that could account for several M > 6 events, close not only in time but also in space. All these issues have led several investigators to study the complex seismotectonics of the southern portion of this region and two views can be summarized as follows.
One interpretation maintains that the Gioia Tauro Plain is a graben, with the Aspromonte Fault as its eastern border and the eastern flank of the Mt. S. Elia horst as its western margin. Such hypothesis is supported by field historical reports contemporary to the 1783 earthquake, that described a 20 km-long fracture bordering the base of the presumed Aspromonte Fault.
Another view by Valensise and D'Addezio (1994) indicates that the the Aspromonte Fault cannot be associated with any clear evidence of offset deposits, thus suggesting it is no longer active, also considering the present-day landscape evolution of the Gioia Tauro Plain. These authors suggest an analogy with the nearby causative fault of the 1908 earthquake in the Messina Straits (to the south). Based on these considerations, we believe that this Source is a relatively young, E-dipping blind normal fault.
The largest portion of this Source has been associated with the 5 February sub-event of the catastrophic 1783 earthquake. For an in-depth analysis of seismogenic processes in this region, the reader may refer to the relevant Individual Source in this Database.
The strike of this Source was based on the model derived from instrumental data, on the distribution of the most recent paleoshorelines and on the local drainage pattern. Also the dip was based on instrumental data and on geological and geometrical considerations. Rake is indicative of pure normal faulting, based on geological and seismological data. The minimum and maximum depth were based on geological and seismological data. Slip rate was inferred from geological observations in adjacent structures that share the same tectonic environment with this Source.

pictures.c: Cotecchia et al.'s [1986] hypothesis for the surface effects of the 5 February 1783 earthquake. The coseismic ruptures at the foot of the Aspromonte are seen as evidence for primary surface faulting. The geometry of the basin filling is admittedly speculative.

pictures.t: Geological map of Gioia Tauro Plain
pictures.c: Simplified geological map of the Gioia Tauro Plain based on published work (from Valensise and D'Addezio [1994]). SectionA-A' as in figure showing"2D comparison of competing faults".

Ghisetti [1984] describes both the Gioia Tauro Plain and the Upper Mesima basins as two graben formed by main west-dipping and secondary east-dipping faults, and points out the existence of transverse structures separating individual basins.

Hypothesis for the geometry of the basin filling resulting from each of the two competing faults, and comparison between the observed gravimetric anomalies and those calculated for the two cases (from Valensise and D'Addezio [1994]).

pictures.t: Calabrian faults from the Neotectonic Map of Italy
pictures.c: The Neotectonic Map of Italy (Ciaranfi et al. [1983]) proposes the existence of a west-dipping, range-bounding normal fault and shows that the whole southern Calabria has been strongly uplifted since the Middle Pleistocene.
Schematic section of the fault systems in the general context of the active Calabrian W-dipping subduction (from Tiberti et al. [2017]).

pictures.t: Overview of the sources [Tiberti et al., 2017]
pictures.c: Overview of the Calabrian sources. Notice that 1. the main normal faults lie antithetic to the subduction plane and host the largest earthquakes, and 2. between 1783 and 1908 large earthquakes ruptured the western extensional domain of the Southern Calabria (from Tiberti et al. [2017]).
